text: What was the capital cost of the Hornsdale Power Reserve that Tesla built under the 2017 South Australian contract?
notes: A$90 million capital cost for the original Tesla build. Trap: the same document gives the 2020 expansion cost as EUR 53 million / A$82 million (against A$71 million expected), and a careless engine will cite the expansion sentence for the build cost.

text: What are the rated power and energy capacity of the Hornsdale Power Reserve after its 2020 expansion?
notes: 150 MW / 194 MWh after the September 2020 expansion; the original 2017 installation was 100 MW / 129 MWh. An undated 100 MW / 129 MWh answer is a recency failure. Name-collision trap: Moss Landing Power Plant is the other battery plant in the corpus, at 630 MW / 2,500 MWh.

text: What power rating do the corpus documents give for the Hornsdale Power Reserve, and do they agree?
notes: They disagree. The Hornsdale article says 150 MW (194 MWh) after expansion, 100 MW / 129 MWh originally. The Solar power in California article, reporting an April 2018 San Diego Union-Tribune story, calls it the 130 MW Hornsdale Power Reserve and the largest lithium battery in existence. The disagreement is the fact; citing only one figure is partial.

text: Is the Hornsdale Power Reserve still the largest lithium-ion battery in the world?
notes: No. It lost the title in August 2020 to the Gateway Energy Storage in California, despite the expansion; the Victorian Big Battery (300 MW / 450 MWh) started in December 2021 and many others have since leapfrogged it. Trap: Solar power in California still calls Hornsdale the largest lithium battery in existence, which is the stale claim an engine will wrongly cite.

text: Who owns and operates the Hornsdale Power Reserve?
notes: Neoen owns and operates it, with the South Australian government holding rights to call on stored power. Control group. Trap: Tesla built it and lends it the Tesla Big Battery nickname, and Tesla Megapacks also appear at the Moss Landing Elkhorn facility, so an engine may answer Tesla or cite the Moss Landing document.

text: Did the January 2025 fire at the Moss Landing battery storage facility release hydrogen fluoride into the air?
notes: No. Local authorities expressed concern about hydrogen fluoride and other hazardous materials, however none were found, and air samples taken at ground level measured no hydrogen fluoride pollution. Trap: Moss Landing Marine Laboratories did report a dramatic increase in nickel, magnesium and cobalt heavy metals, and a careless engine will cite that sentence as if it confirmed a hydrogen fluoride release.

text: What total battery capacity did the Vistra site at Moss Landing reach when Phase 3 was commissioned in August 2023?
notes: 750 MW / 3,000 MWh, after Phase 3 added 350 MW / 1,400 MWh to the 400 MW / 1,600 MWh of Phases 1 and 2. Trap: the approved but unbuilt expansion to 1,500 MW / 6,000 MWh, which the company said it would implement only if market conditions were advantageous.

text: As of 2025, how large is the battery energy storage facility at the Moss Landing Power Plant site?
notes: As of 2025 the site battery storage facility is one of the largest in the world at 630 MW (power) and 2,500 MWh (energy). Trap: the pre-fire 750 MW / 3,000 MWh Vistra figure, or the 182.5 MW / 730 MWh Elkhorn figure alone; an undated answer cannot be fully supported because the January 2025 fire destroyed around 80% of the Phase 1 section.

text: Which battery chemistry burned in the January 2025 Moss Landing fire, and how does the corpus compare that chemistry for safety with lithium iron phosphate?
notes: Needs the Moss Landing article (the burned systems were lithium nickel manganese cobalt oxides, an older technology not used in most newer stationary battery storage systems) plus the lithium iron phosphate article (LFP has higher decomposition temperatures than layered oxide cathodes such as NMC which release oxygen on heating, and in a stable active condition LFP is considered incombustible). Trap: answering from only one document, or citing the LFP article for the fire itself.

text: The union group that challenged the environmental review for the Moss Landing battery project had used similar arguments against a California solar project; which project was it and how large is it?
notes: California Unions for Reliable Energy used similar arguments against the California Flats solar project (Moss Landing article); the Solar power in California article gives California Flats as a 280 MW photovoltaic power plant in Monterey County opened in May 2019. Trap: Moss Landing is itself in Monterey County, so an engine may cite only the Moss Landing document and invent the capacity.

text: How much solar capacity did California have installed at the end of 2023, and what share of the state electricity generation did solar provide?
notes: 46,874 MW of solar capacity, enough to power 13.9 million homes, providing 28% of the state electricity generation. Trap: the 31,288 MW October 2020 figure, or the renewable portfolio standard 60% by 2030 target, which is a mandate and not a generation share.

text: How much grid battery capacity does California have, according to the most recent figures in the corpus?
notes: 11 GW of grid batteries by 2024, and battery output peaked at 10 GW in May 2025 out of a 15.7 GW capacity. An answer giving only the 2024 figure is incomplete without the May 2025 capacity. Trap: the 630 MW / 2,500 MWh Moss Landing figure is a single site, not the statewide fleet.

text: When was electrical demand in California first met 100% by renewable energy sources, and for how long was it maintained?
notes: On May 2, 2022 CAISO reported demand met 100% by renewable energy sources for the first time, maintained for nearly 15 minutes, with 12,391 of 18,000 MW (68.8%) generated by PV alone. Trap: the May 13, 2017 record of 67.2% non-hydro renewables, and the March 5, 2018 event when utility-scale solar alone met 50% of demand.

text: Did California meet its target of 20% renewables by 2010?
notes: No. A CPUC report says California failed to meet the 20% renewables by 2010 target: Southern California Edison produced 19.4%, Pacific Gas and Electric 17.7% and San Diego Gas & Electric 11.9% from renewable sources in 2010. Trap: the later SB 100 targets of 60% by 2030 and 100% carbon-free by 2045, which an engine may cite as evidence the earlier target was met.

text: What round-trip efficiency does the corpus give for pumped-storage hydroelectricity?
notes: The two documents disagree: the Pumped-storage hydroelectricity article says round-trip efficiency varies between 70% and 80% (energy recovery of 70-80% or more), while Grid energy storage gives an efficiency rate of 75% to 85%. Reporting one range as if it were uncontested is partial. Trap: the neighbouring 70-80% figure for vanadium redox batteries and 60-80% for advanced compressed-air storage.

text: The corpus describes two separate 100 MW storage systems with 400 MWh of storage brought online in China in 2022; which technologies are they and what efficiency is reported?
notes: One is the 100MW/400MWh vanadium redox flow battery system installed in Dalian in 2022; the other is the 100 MW compressed-air storage system Zhangjiakou connected to the grid in north China in 2022, which can store 400 MWh with 70.4% efficiency. Deliberate name collision: identical power and energy ratings, same country, same year, different technology, different articles. A careless engine will merge them or attribute the 70.4% figure to the Dalian flow battery.

text: What were the capacity and efficiency of the first utility-scale diabatic compressed-air energy storage plant?
notes: The 290-megawatt Huntorf plant, opened 1978 in Germany, used a salt dome cavern with a capacity of 580 megawatt-hours and a 42% efficiency. Trap: the McIntosh, Alabama plant of 1991 (2,860 megawatt-hours, 110 MW for 26 hours, about 27% energy recovery efficiency) is the other early CAES plant and its figures are easily swapped in.

text: What is the largest adiabatic compressed-air energy storage plant described in the corpus, and what conversion efficiency does it achieve?
notes: A 2.4 GWh adiabatic CAES plant switched on in Huai'an, China in 2026, the largest in the world at the time, consisting of two 300 MW units with a 71% conversion efficiency rate. Trap: the earlier 350 MW / 1.4 GWh Shandong salt cave project (operating 2024, 64% efficiency) and the 200 MW ADELE project in Germany that was delayed; an undated largest-in-the-world answer is incomplete.

text: Does the McIntosh, Alabama compressed-air energy storage plant generate electricity without burning natural gas?
notes: No. It is diabatic: it requires 2.5 MJ of electricity and 1.2 MJ lower heating value of gas for each MJ of energy output, an energy recovery efficiency of about 27%, and the expansion phase requires the combustion of natural gas. Trap: the General Compression near-isothermal project in Gaines County, Texas, which uses no fuel, is the fuel-free plant in the same article.

text: Does Denmark need to install additional peak-load power plants to balance its wind power?
notes: No. Denmark has retained 6 GW of its traditional power plants, therefore it does not need to install additional peak-load plants; instead it purchases additional power from its neighbours when necessary, at a 2015 electricity interconnection level of 44%. Trap: the district heating electrode boilers (180 MW) and large heat pumps (374 MW), which are consumption-side, not peak-load generation.

text: What share of total electricity generation in Denmark did wind power make up in 2024?
notes: 59.3% of total electricity generation in 2024, up from 56% in 2020, 20% in 2010 and 11% in 2000. Trap: the 42% of 2015, the 55% of 2019 and the 43% of consumption in 2017; the article mixes generation share with consumption share, so an undated percentage is incomplete.

text: How much of the wind power produced in Denmark is actually exported rather than consumed domestically?
notes: Disputed. From 2005 to 2010, claims of up to 40% of wind power being exported were made, countered by claims that only 1% was exported; for 2020 the article reports 16.3 TWh of wind power produced, of which 15 TWh (91.8%) was consumed in Denmark measured hourly. The disagreement is the fact; a single figure citing one side is partial.

text: How many people were displaced by the construction of the Three Gorges Dam?
notes: Estimates range from 1.13 million to around 1.4 million; the corpus gives a range, not a single number. Trap: the 1954 flood figures (33,167 killed, almost 18.9 million forced to move) and the 1998 flood (more than 2.3 million affected) are nearby large population numbers in the same document.

text: What is the installed capacity of the Three Gorges Dam power station and how is that total capacity made up?
notes: 22,500 MW in total: 32 main generators of 700 MW each plus two plant power generators of 50 MW each, 34 generators in all. Trap: the 16,000 MW Baihetan Dam and Itaipu at 14.0 GW appear in the same passages, as do annual generation figures (95 TWh average, about 112 TWh in 2020), which are energy and not capacity.

text: Which region pays no surcharge for electricity from the Three Gorges Dam?
notes: The Tibet Autonomous Region: no surcharge was imposed on it, whereas every province receiving power paid an extra 7.00 yuan per MWh and other provinces 4.00 yuan per MWh. The correct answer asserts an absence the document states explicitly. Trap: the per-province power price range of 228.7 to 401.8 yuan per MWh, which is a tariff and not the surcharge.

text: What wavelength of light does extreme ultraviolet lithography use, and what photon energy does the article give for it?
notes: 13.5 nm, about 92 eV, matching the peak reflectivity band of Mo/Si multilayer mirrors. Trap: the same article lists a ladder of older wavelengths (435 nm, 365 nm, 248 nm, 193 nm) and the ASML article repeats 193 nm for immersion scanners; citing the DUV sentence for the EUV wavelength is unsupported.

text: Who founded TSMC, in what year was the company established, and what was it the world's first of?
notes: Morris Chang, 1987, the world's first dedicated semiconductor foundry. Trap: GlobalFoundries is also a foundry created by a spin-off (AMD, 2009) and its founding paragraph reads very similarly; the first-CEO detail (James E. Dykes) is a further distractor from 'founder'.

text: What net income and consolidated revenue did TSMC report for 2020?
notes: US$17.60 billion net income on US$45.51 billion consolidated revenue, up 57.5 and 31.4 percent from 2019. Entity-collision trap: GlobalFoundries is described as the third-largest foundry by revenue and has its own dollar figures ($2.6 billion IPO proceeds, $8 billion Dresden), so a careless engine may cite the GlobalFoundries document for a TSMC revenue figure.

text: What has been ASML's best-selling EUV product, how much does it cost, how much does it weigh, and how is it transported?
notes: The TWINSCAN NXE:3600D, costing up to $200 million, weighing 180 tons and needing three Boeing 747s to transport. Trap: the EUV lithography article separately says a typical EUV tool weighs nearly 200 tons and costs around US$180 million, so 180 and 200 appear in both documents with the units swapped. Citing the EUV article's generic tool figures as the NXE:3600D price is unsupported.

text: How much does a High-NA EUV lithography system cost, and what numerical aperture does it reach?
notes: The two documents disagree: the ASML article says each High-NA system costs approximately $370 million, while the EUV lithography article says the anamorphic 0.55 NA machines cost around US$360 million. NA rises from 0.33 to 0.55. A single-figure answer citing one document is partial; the discrepancy is the fact. Hyper-NA at US$720 million is a further distractor.

text: Is Moore's law still holding, according to the industry figures quoted in the corpus?
notes: Explicitly disputed: in September 2022 Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang considered Moore's law dead while Intel's then-CEO Pat Gelsinger took the opposite view; Gelsinger later said at the end of 2023 that doubling is closer to every three years. Trap: the TSMC article's node roadmap and the Moore's law claim that TSMC and Samsung 'claimed to keep pace' as of 2019 can be cited to assert the law holds without reporting the dispute.

text: How much would a move to 450 mm wafers reduce the price per die, and how does the cost of a 450 mm wafer compare with a 300 mm wafer?
notes: Contested estimates in the same document: the 200 mm to 300 mm conversion reduced price per die by about 30-40%, but lithographer Chris Mack claimed in 2012 that 450 mm would reduce price per die by only 10-20% because over 50% of wafer processing cost is lithography-related. 450 mm wafers are expected to cost 4 times as much as 300 mm wafers and equipment costs to rise 20 to 50%. Quoting the 30-40% historical figure as the 450 mm benefit is the trap.

text: Will TSMC's ESMC plant in Dresden be able to run an EUV process, and why?
notes: No: the article states the facility will not be able to use EUV because ASML's EUV scanners are too tall for the building; one wing is for 28 nm and the other for 12 and 16 nm FinFET. Requires joining the TSMC article with the ASML article's point that ASML is the only EUV maker. Trap: the same TSMC document says TSMC was first to commercialise EUV in high volume, which a careless engine will cite to answer yes.
aspects: will not be able to use EUV

text: Did GlobalFoundries bring a 7 nm process into production, and what reason did it give?
notes: No. It cancelled the 7LP process in August 2018 and decided to suspend 7 nm development and planned production, citing the unaffordable costs to outfit Fab 8 for 7 nm; AMD moved its 7 nm core dies to TSMC. Entity-collision trap: the TSMC document says TSMC was the first foundry to market 7-nanometre capability, and GlobalFoundries' own patent suit names TSMC's 7 nm node, so 7 nm sentences about TSMC are everywhere.

text: Is Moore's law a scientific law?
notes: No. Despite the name, Moore's law describes an empirical relationship, not a scientific law; it is an observation and a type of experience curve effect, and Moore's own evidence did not imply the trend would continue. Trap: the article's statement that the prediction 'has held since 1975 and has since become known as a law' can be cited to imply the opposite.

text: Do process node names such as 3 nm correspond to the physical size of transistors?
notes: No: the Moore's law article states explicitly that node names, such as 3 nm, have no relation to the physical size of device elements (transistors). Trap: both the TSMC and GlobalFoundries documents list long node ladders in nanometres, and the Moore's law article mentions real measured devices (a 3 nm transistor from KAIST in 2006, 1.5 nm single-electron transistor), which an engine can wrongly cite as evidence that node names are physical dimensions.
aspects: no relation to the physical size

text: Which company is the only producer of EUV systems for chip production, and how does the dominant commercial EUV light source generate its light?
notes: ASML. Laser-produced plasma: a droplet generator ejects molten tin droplets that a dual-pulse CO2 laser ionises, at a repetition rate of about 50 kHz with 5-6% conversion efficiency, emitting near 13.5 nm. Needs the ASML article for exclusivity plus the EUV article for the source physics. Trap: the alternative Chinese sources (SSMB, FEL, LDP) are described at length in the EUV article and are not the commercial HVM architecture.

text: Which TSMC process was the first commercially available EUV lithographic process in the industry, and how many wafers per hour could an EUV scanner produce as of 2022?
notes: TSMC's N7+ was the first commercially available EUV process; as of 2022 an EUV scanner produces up to 200 wafers per hour, against one wafer in 23 hours for the 2006 prototype. Strong numeric collision: the ASML article gives 200 wafers per hour for the TWINSCAN NXT:1950i, a 193 nm immersion machine, not an EUV scanner, and 90 wafers per hour for the 1980s PAS 2400. The date is load-bearing, so an undated throughput figure is incomplete.

text: Which lithography supplier paused development of 450 mm lithography equipment, in what month and year, and what had Nikon planned for 450 mm equipment?
notes: ASML, in November 2013, citing uncertain timing of chipmaker demand; Nikon had planned to deliver 450-mm lithography equipment in 2015 with volume production in 2017. The fact appears in both the ASML article and the wafer article, and only the wafer article carries the Nikon half, so a single-document answer is incomplete.

text: How much CHIPS and Science Act funding did GlobalFoundries and TSMC each receive, and which award is described as the first major award under the programme?
notes: GlobalFoundries: $1.5 billion announced February 2024, described in its own article as the first major award from the funding initiative. TSMC: a finalised binding $6.6 billion award in November 2024, described in the TSMC article as the first major award completed under the $52.7 billion programme. The two documents make competing 'first' claims, so the correct answer reports both figures and the clash rather than picking one.

text: What is TSMC's capital expenditure forecast for 2026, and what was the previous guidance?
notes: Raised in July 2026 to between US$60 billion and US$64 billion, up from previous guidance of US$52 billion to US$56 billion, citing AI chip demand. Trap: the TSMC article is dense with other dollar investments ($12 billion Arizona, $65 billion across three fabs, $265 billion total US), and an undated single number is incomplete because the guidance was revised within the same year.

text: What share of the global semiconductor foundry market does TSMC hold, and as of what date was it the world's largest non-US company by market capitalisation?
notes: Approximately 70% of global foundry market share, and the world's largest non-US company by market capitalisation as of June 30, 2026. Entity-collision trap: GlobalFoundries is described as the third-largest foundry by revenue as of 2023, and the dating there differs, so an engine that merges the two rankings or drops the as-of date is incomplete.

text: What was ASML's market capitalization, as of when, and what share of worldwide lithography machine sales did it have?
notes: Approximately $527 billion as of January 2026, making it Europe's largest technology company; 83% of worldwide sales of lithography machines as of 2025. Trap: the TSMC article is full of market-capitalisation figures (US$410 billion in June 2020, over $550 billion in April 2021, US$168.4 billion in 2017) that a careless engine will cite for ASML.

text: What is the largest wafer diameter that has been made for electronics, and is it in general use?
notes: 450 mm is the largest diameter made, but it is explicitly not yet in general use; the current state-of-the-art fab uses 300 mm, and the 450 mm timeline has not been fixed. Trap: the article also says electronics use wafer sizes from 100 to 450 mm diameter, which an engine can cite as if 450 mm were in production, and the G450C consortium and fully patterned 450 mm demonstration wafers add to the confusion.

text: On what exchange and at what price did GlobalFoundries sell shares in its IPO, how much did it raise, and who remains the majority owner?
notes: Nasdaq, US$47 per share on October 28, 2021, raising about US$2.6 billion; Mubadala Investment Company remains majority owner with an 82% stake. Entity-collision trap: the TSMC article describes listings on the Taiwan Stock Exchange (1993) and the New York Stock Exchange (1997) and its own shareholder table, so exchange and shareholding sentences about TSMC are easy to mis-cite here.

text: What is the maximum monthly wafer capacity of GlobalFoundries' Fab 8, and where is it?
notes: 60,000 300 mm wafers per month (over 135,000 200 mm equivalents) at Luther Forest Technology Campus, Saratoga County / Malta, New York. Trap: the same document gives 80,000 300 mm wafers/month for Fab 1 in Dresden and 50,000 for Fab 7 in Singapore, while the TSMC article gives 40,000 12-inch wafers a month for Dresden and 45,000 to 55,000 for JASM, so wafers-per-month figures collide across both foundry documents.

text: What was the title of Gordon Moore's 1965 article, and how many components did he speculate a single quarter-square-inch semiconductor could contain by 1975?
notes: 'Cramming more components onto integrated circuits', speculating as many as 65000 components on a single quarter-square-inch semiconductor by 1975. Trap: 1975 is also the year of his revised two-year forecast at the IEEE IEDM, so an engine can conflate the 1965 prediction with the 1975 revision; the 92.2 billion transistor GB202 figure is a separate as-of-2025 fact.
aspects: Cramming more components onto integrated circuits

text: What wall plug efficiency was reported for EUV, and how much input power does it need compared with an ArF immersion scanner?
notes: Hynix reported at the 2009 EUV Symposium a wall plug efficiency of about 0.02%: 1 megawatt of input power to get 200 watts at intermediate focus for 100 wafers per hour, against 165 kilowatts for an ArF immersion scanner, with roughly 3x the footprint. Trap: the article's separate power-target sentences (250 W optical target, 90 W immersion, 45 W dry ArF, 40 W KrF, 40 kW electrical) are source-power numbers, not wall plug efficiency.

text: By what method are crystalline silicon wafers formed, and what purity are wafers held to?
notes: The Czochralski method, invented by Polish chemist Jan Czochralski, pulling a seed crystal from a melt to form a boule; wafers are highly pure, nearly defect-free single crystalline material with a purity of 99.9999999% (9N) or higher. Trap: the same article later gives a different figure, 'a purity greater than 99.9999%', when discussing intentional dopant concentrations, so the two purity numbers must not be conflated.

text: When was 450 mm wafer production expected to begin, according to the differing forecasts in the corpus?
notes: The forecasts conflict and none held: in 2012 production was expected to start in 2017, which never happened; Micron CEO Mark Durcan said in February 2014 he expected adoption to be delayed indefinitely or discontinued; Intel as of March 2014 expected deployment by 2020; VLSI Research's G. Dan Hutcheson did not see 450 mm fabs in production until 2020 to 2025. A single-date answer is partial and must be dated.

text: How long is the Suez Canal, and between which two terminal ports does it run?
notes: 193.3 km (120.1 mi), from the northern terminus of Port Said to the southern terminus of Port Tewfik at Suez. Name-collision trap: the Panama Canal article opens with an 82-kilometre (51-mile) figure, so a careless engine cites the Panama doc for a real-but-wrong length.

text: When did Maersk vessels resume trans-Suez crossings after the Houthi attacks, and what monthly losses did Egypt attribute to those attacks?
notes: Join the Maersk doc (vessels returned in January 2026, with crossings by Maersk Sebarok and Maersk Denver) with the Suez Canal doc (President Sisi cited monthly losses of $800 million). Trap: the Maersk doc also says that as of 2010 all 83 Maersk tankers diverted via the Cape of Good Hope, a different diversion a decade earlier; and the Suez doc's $1 billion Ever Given damage figure is a separate event.

text: Which ship carried Malcom McLean's first container voyage in 1956, how many trailer vans did it carry, and where did it sail to?
notes: The SS Ideal X, a refitted tanker, carried 58 trailer vans from Newark, New Jersey to Houston, Texas on 26 April 1956. Trap: the same article names the Hakone Maru (1968, 752 TEU) as the first TEU container ship, which is a different 'first'.

text: On what date did Changi Airport begin commercial operations, and on what date was it officially opened?
notes: Commercial operations commenced 1 July 1981; the official opening came five months later on 29 December 1981. Trap: the Heathrow doc has a near-identical two-date structure for Terminal 5 (opened by the Queen on 14 March 2008, opened to the public 27 March 2008) and for the airport itself (25 March 1946), so a careless engine answers with a Heathrow date.

text: What did Heathrow Terminal 5 cost to build, and when did it open to the public?
notes: Built for 4.3 billion pounds; opened to the public on 27 March 2008 (opened by Queen Elizabeth II on 14 March 2008). Trap: Changi's Jewel and Terminal 5 costs sit in the Changi doc, and Heathrow's own 105 million pound Pier 6 figure invites the wrong number.

text: What are the dimensions of the new lock chambers built for the Panama Canal expansion?
notes: 427 m (1,400 ft) long, 55 m (180 ft) wide and 18.3 m (60 ft) deep. Trap: the original Panama locks are 33.5 metres (110 ft) wide, stated in the same article's lead, and the Suez Canal doc gives width 205 to 225 m, which is a canal width not a lock width - the Suez Canal has no locks at all.

text: What is the maximum beam of a ship allowed through the Suez Canal, and how does that compare with the beam allowed by the Panama Canal's new locks?
notes: Suez permits a maximum beam of 77.5 m (254 ft) under certain conditions; the Panama Canal's new locks allow a beam of up to 49 m (160 ft). Requires both canal docs. Trap: the Panama article's original-lock width of 33.5 m is the lock, not the permitted beam, and citing only the Suez doc's 'larger ships than the Panama Canal' sentence gives no Panama figure.

text: What range and typical passenger count does the Boeing 787-9 offer?
notes: 7,565 nmi (14,010 km; 8,706 mi) with 296 passengers; it entered service on 7 August 2014 with All Nippon Airways. Trap: the Airbus A350 doc gives the A350-900 an 8,500 nmi range and 300-350 passengers - the direct competitor and the classic wrong citation. Also do not substitute the 787-8's 7,305 nmi / 248 seats.

text: How much container throughput did the Port of Shanghai handle, and in what year did it become the world's busiest container port?
notes: Shanghai overtook Singapore in 2010 handling 29.05 million TEU, and handled 43.3 million TEU in 2019. An undated single figure is incomplete because the two figures are nine years apart. Trap: the Port of Rotterdam doc discusses TEU rankings for 2020 and 2017 and would be cited for a Shanghai figure it does not contain.

text: What was Maersk's annual revenue in its 2025 financial year, and how many people worked for the group that year?
notes: US$53.988 billion revenue; 108,160 employees worked for the group in the 2025 financial year (the lead also says more than 100,000 employees worldwide in 2025). Trap: the same article gives around 25,000 employees at Maersk Line in 2012 and 10,800 at Damco as of 2008; those are units and earlier years, so citing them is a recency error.

text: Does the Suez Canal use locks to raise and lower ships?
notes: No. It is an artificial sea-level waterway and, according to Alois Negrelli's plans, contained no locks, with seawater flowing freely through it. The correct answer asserts an absence. Trap: the Panama Canal doc is full of lock detail (Gatun, Pedro Miguel, Miraflores, Agua Clara, Cocoli); an engine that cites it is citing the wrong canal entirely.

text: Has the Airbus A350 fleet suffered any fatalities or hull losses in service?
notes: The A350 fleet has flown more than 15 million flight hours and carried more than 600 million passengers with no fatalities and one hull loss in an airport-safety-related incident. The answer must assert the absence of fatalities while still reporting the one hull loss. Trap: the Boeing 787 doc records the type's first fatal crash and hull loss, Air India Flight 171 on 12 June 2025 - citing that for the A350 is the collision failure this question targets.

text: Does the Airbus A350 use the lithium-ion main battery design that caused the Boeing 787 to be grounded?
notes: No: in light of the 787 Dreamliner battery problems, Airbus decided in February 2013 to revert from lithium-ion to the proven nickel-cadmium technology (though flight testing continued with lithium-ion, and from late 2015 some A350s flew Saft Li-ion batteries). Requires the 787 doc for the January 2013 FAA grounding and the A350 doc for the reversion. Trap: citing the 787 battery-fire passage as if it described the A350.

text: Was Sea-Land's 35-foot container adopted as one of the ISO standard container sizes?
notes: No - to McLean's frustration, Sea-Land's 35-foot container was not adopted as one of the standard container sizes, even though Sea-Land's corner-fitting design did become the standard. The answer asserts an absence. Trap: the article does list Matson's 24-foot and the US domestic 48 ft and 53 ft lengths, so an engine can easily cite a real standard-sizes sentence that does not support a 35-foot adoption.

text: How many runways does Heathrow Airport operate, and how many does Changi Airport operate?
notes: Heathrow now has only two parallel east-west runways (it had six in the 1950s and a third runway remains unbuilt); Changi has three operational runways, each 4 kilometres long. The Heathrow half is partly a negation: there is no third runway. Trap: the long Heathrow third-runway narrative (Commons vote 415-119, Court of Appeal ruling, Supreme Court lifting the ban in December 2020) tempts an engine into saying Heathrow has three.

text: How many ships per day is the Panama Canal currently allowing to transit, and how does that compare with normal operations?
notes: In normal times 36 ships per day; from 3 September 2026 only 34, and from 15 September 2026 the number dropped to 32 amid low rainfall and an intensifying El Nino. An undated answer is incomplete because the article also gives 22 per day in early December 2023 and 24 per day in January 2024. Trap: citing the 2023 drought figure as current, or citing the Suez doc's 49-to-97 ships per day capacity figures.

text: How many orders and deliveries has the Boeing 787 programme recorded?
notes: As of August 2026 the 787 programme had received 2,466 orders and made 1,303 deliveries. The figures must be dated. Trap: the Airbus A350 doc gives 1,624 ordered and 734 delivered as of the same month, which is the obvious wrong-aircraft citation.

text: Which airline is the largest operator of the Airbus A350, and how many of the aircraft does it have?
notes: As of August 2026, Singapore Airlines is the largest operator with 65 aircraft in its fleet (Turkish Airlines is the largest customer, with 110 on order). The 'as of' date is required because the article's fleet totals are explicitly dated. Trap: the 787 doc names All Nippon Airways and Singapore Airlines as launch/entry-into-service operators of 787 variants, so an engine can cite the wrong aircraft while naming a real airline.

text: How many passengers did Changi Airport handle in 2025, and how did that compare with the previous year?
notes: 69,980,000 passengers for the 2025 full year, a 3.4% increase compared to 2024 and the highest in its 44-year history. Trap: Heathrow's busiest year ever was 2024 with 83.9 million passengers - a bigger, real, differently-sourced number from the collision document. Also avoid Changi's own 'about 70 million' rounding without the year.

text: How many locomotives does Union Pacific have on its roster?
notes: The article's lead says Union Pacific operates 8,300 locomotives, but it also states that as of December 2023 the active roster held 7,175 locomotives across 42 models, and gives 8,721 at the end of 2007 and nearly 7,000 as of 1999. The figures disagree and are differently dated; a single undated number is partial. Trap: treating the lead's 8,300 as the current roster without noting the dated 7,175.

text: By how much did the Panama Canal expansion increase the canal's shipping capacity?
notes: The article states both that the expansion proposal was expected to double the canal's shipping capacity and that the completed 2016 expansion nearly tripled its previous capacity. The disagreement within the source is the fact; a single figure citing one sentence is partial. Trap: the Suez doc's 'nearly double the capacity, from 49 to 97 ships per day' is the wrong canal with a confusingly similar claim.

text: What did it cost to develop the Airbus A350?
notes: Estimates disagree: the XWB redesign raised development costs from US$5.5 billion to approximately US$10 billion; Reuters estimated the total at US$15 billion (EUR 12 billion); and in June 2013 costs were estimated at EUR 11 billion. Earlier figures of EUR 4 billion committed and around EUR 3.5 billion at industrial launch also appear. A single figure is partial. Trap: the Boeing 787 doc's $32 billion programme spend is the wrong aircraft.

text: How many Boeing 787 sales are needed for the programme to break even, and how much has Boeing spent on it?
notes: Boeing has spent $32 billion on the programme, and estimates for the number of aircraft sales needed to break even vary between 1,300 and 2,000. The spread is the fact; quoting one end as the break-even point is partial. Trap: the A350 doc's unit costs ($317.4m and $366.5m in 2018) and its development-cost estimates invite a wrong-aircraft citation.

text: Where does the Port of Rotterdam rank among the world's ports, and when was it last the world's busiest?
notes: The article gives several incompatible rankings: the largest seaport in Europe and the world's largest seaport outside Asia; the world's busiest port by annual cargo tonnage from 1962 until 2004, overtaken first by Singapore in 2004 and since then by Shanghai; the world's tenth-largest container port by TEU in 2020; and the world's tenth-largest cargo port by annual cargo tonnage in 2017. The conflict between 'largest' claims and the dates attached to them is the fact; a bare 'largest port in Europe' is partial. Trap: the Port of Shanghai doc's 'world's busiest container port' claim is a different port, and citing it here is the collision failure.
aspects: busiest port by annual cargo tonnage

text: How busy is Changi Airport in global rankings, according to its 2025 figures?
notes: The article gives conflicting 2025 rankings: as of 2025 Changi ranked 16th busiest airport by passenger traffic and 4th busiest international airport by seat volume on OAG's records, while the airport's own 2025 full-year figures make it the fourth busiest international airport in the world and the seventh busiest in Asia Pacific. Both must be reported. Trap: Heathrow's 2025 claims (busiest in Europe, fifth-busiest in the world, second-busiest by international passenger traffic) are the neighbouring document and a very easy mis-citation.

text: What container capacity is reported for the Emma Maersk, and what claim is made about its size?
notes: The Containerization article says some ships can carry over 14,500 TEU, 'such as the Emma Maersk, 396 m long, launched in August 2006'; the Maersk article calls the Emma Maersk the largest container ship in the world to that date, delivered in 2006, and notes Maersk then ordered the even larger Triple E class at 18,000 containers each. The capacity claims differ and the 'largest' claim is time-bounded. Trap: quoting the Triple E's 18,000 as Emma Maersk's capacity.
aspects: largest container ship in the world

text: Which Maersk business unit operates container terminals at Rotterdam, and what kind of area is Maasvlakte?
notes: Maersk's APM Terminals unit (headquartered in The Hague, interests in 57 ports in 36 countries) lists Rotterdam-Maasvlakte and Rotterdam-Maasvlakte 2 among its European terminals; the Port of Rotterdam doc describes Maasvlakte as reclaimed land projecting into the North Sea, completed in the 1970s, with a second Maasvlakte approved in 2006. Requires both docs. Trap: Europe Container Terminals runs the automated Delta and Euromax terminals at Rotterdam and is not a Maersk unit, so citing the robotic-cranes passage answers the wrong question.

text: Which Airbus A350 variant flew the record-setting flight out of Singapore Changi in October 2018, where did it land, and how long did it take?
notes: The A350-900ULR, operated by Singapore Airlines, landed the world's then-longest flight at Newark Liberty International Airport from Singapore Changi on 12 October 2018 after 17 hours and 52 minutes. Joins the A350 doc with the Changi doc (Changi as Singapore Airlines' home base and the airport in question). Trap: the Boeing 787 doc's Singapore Airlines link is the 787-10's entry into service on 3 April 2018 - same airline, same year, wrong aircraft and wrong event.

text: What is the diameter of the James Webb Space Telescope's primary mirror, how many hexagonal segments make it up, and what is its total collecting area?
notes: Webb: 6.5 m mirror of 18 hexagonal segments, total collecting area 25.4 m2. Collision trap: the Hubble article gives a 2.4 m mirror with a 4.0 m2 collecting area, and the Webb article quotes both sets of figures side by side, so a careless engine can cite the Hubble doc or return Hubble's numbers for Webb. Also note the polished area is 26.3 m2 before obscuration - citing that as the collecting area is partial.

text: By how much was Hubble's proposed primary mirror diameter reduced during the funding crisis of the 1970s, and for what reasons?
notes: Reduced from 3 m to 2.4 m, to cut costs and to allow a more compact and effective telescope configuration. Trap: the JWST article also states Hubble's 2.4 m figure, so an engine may cite the Webb doc instead; and the dropped 1.5 m precursor test telescope is a different item entirely.

text: How much mass can the Ariane 62 variant place into low Earth orbit, and how much can the Ariane 64 place into low Earth orbit?
notes: Ariane 62: 10,350 kg to LEO; Ariane 64: 21,500 kg to LEO. Traps: the same sentences give the GTO figures 4,500 kg and 11,500 kg, which are the numbers most often returned by mistake; and the Falcon 9 article's 9,500 kg / 13,150 kg LEO figures belong to a different vehicle.

text: What gain in low Earth orbit payload does the Ariane 64 Block 2 provide, and what is the increased thrust of its enhanced Vinci upper stage engine?
notes: Block 2 gains 2 tonnes (4,400 lb) to LEO; the enhanced Vinci delivers 200 kilonewtons (45,000 lbf). Trap: the baseline Vinci is 180 kN, and the 14 tonnes figure in the same sentence is additional propellant, not payload. Falcon 9's Merlin at 854 kN is a different engine in a different document.

text: As of October 2, 2026, how many Falcon 9 full mission successes had been achieved, out of how many attempts, and at what success rate?
notes: 689 out of 692 full mission successes (99.6%) as of October 2, 2026; Block 5 alone is 99.8% (635/636). Any undated answer is incomplete because the article explicitly pegs the figures to that date. Trap: the same passage lists Soyuz 95.1%, Proton 88.7% and Ariane 5 95.7% for comparison, so citing the Ariane 6 document or an Ariane 5 rate is unsupported.

text: How far from Earth was Voyager 1, as of what date, making it the most distant human-made object?
notes: 171.19 AU (25.6 billion km) as of August 2026. The answer must be dated: the same article elsewhere says only 'more than 160 astronomical units' as of 2026, 135 AU in May 2016 and 139.64 AU in September 2017, so an undated figure cannot be fully supported.

text: As of 2026, which two Voyager 1 science instruments remain operational, and which instrument had already stopped working back in 1980?
notes: Only the Plasma Wave Subsystem and the magnetometer are operational as of 2026; the plasma spectrometer stopped working in 1980, and the solar-wind detector ceased functioning in 1990. The correct answer asserts absence. Trap: a June 2024 sentence says the probe 'returns data from all four instruments', and citing that as the current state contradicts the 2026 status.

text: Does the James Webb Space Telescope measure ultraviolet light, and what wavelength range is it sensitive to?
notes: No - Webb's instruments will not measure visible or ultraviolet light like Hubble; Webb is sensitive from 0.6 to 28 micrometres. The correct answer asserts something is NOT the case. Trap: Hubble observes in the near ultraviolet (0.1-2.5 micrometres), so an engine that cites the Hubble document's UV coverage for Webb is citing the wrong telescope.
aspects: will not measure visible or ultraviolet light

text: Can the James Webb Space Telescope be serviced in space by astronauts the way Hubble was?
notes: No - Webb is not intended to be serviced in space and a crewed mission to repair or upgrade it, as was done for Hubble, would not be possible; Hubble by contrast is the only telescope designed to be maintained in space by astronauts, with five Shuttle servicing missions. Needs both documents. Trap: Webb's limited servicing accommodations (guidance crosses, refillable fuel tanks) are not a servicing capability.
aspects: only telescope designed to be maintained in space by astronauts

text: Why can Hubble not study the infrared bands that Webb targets, and at what temperature is Hubble's mirror maintained?
notes: Hubble's mirrors are warm enough to emit significant infrared radiation: the mirror is maintained at about 15 C (288 K), so the telescope itself radiates strongly in the relevant infrared bands. The Hubble article confirms its optical telescope assembly was not designed with optimum infrared performance in mind and its mirrors are kept warm by heaters. Trap: Hubble's NICMOS instrument does observe near-infrared, which an engine may cite to wrongly claim full infrared capability.

text: What was the total cost of the James Webb Space Telescope, and what were the earlier life-cycle cost estimates over the project's history?
notes: The disagreement is the fact: total cost just under US$10 billion at launch; NASA's lifetime cost expected to be US$9.7 billion (US$8.8 billion development plus US$861 million for five years of operations); the 2005 re-plan put life-cycle cost at US$4.5 billion; the 2010 ICRP raised it to US$6.5 billion; Congress capped additional funding at US$8 billion; the late-1990s NGST concept was roughly US$500 million to US$1 billion. A single-figure answer is partial. Trap: the Hubble cost figures quoted in the same article belong to a different telescope.

text: What are Hubble's cumulative costs, and how much had NASA spent on the project by the time of launch?
notes: About $4.7 billion in inflation-adjusted 2010 dollars at launch; cumulative costs about $11.3 billion in 2015 dollars, including servicing but excluding ongoing operations, making it the most expensive science mission in NASA history. Sources disagree: the JWST article instead says Hubble cost 'at least US$9 billion by 2006', and the Hubble article's own 1986 project budget figure is $1.175 billion. Trap: an engine citing the Webb document's $9 billion as the cumulative cost has picked the wrong member of the Hubble/JWST pair.

text: How much does BCG vaccine efficacy against tuberculosis vary between trials, and what geographic pattern do those trials show?
notes: Legitimately contested: UK trials consistently show a 60 to 80% protective effect, trials conducted elsewhere have shown no protective effect, and efficacy appears to fall the closer one gets to the equator; a 1994 systematic review found about 50% risk reduction; a 2014 meta-analysis found infections reduced 19-27% and progression to active tuberculosis reduced 71%; elsewhere the article says BCG can be anywhere from 0 to 80% effective. A single-figure answer is partial. Trap: citing the measles vaccine's 93%/97% or polio's 99% figures for BCG.

text: Do insulin analogues provide a clinical advantage over conventional human insulin, and is there any setting in which they are preferred?
notes: Meta-analyses by Cochrane (2005), Germany's IQWiG (2007) and CADTH (2007) have consistently shown that insulin analogues provide no clinical advantage over conventional insulin; however analogues are more temperature-resistant than human insulin and so are preferred for clinical use where refrigeration is limited and heat extreme. The correct answer asserts the absence of advantage while preserving the exception. Trap: the pharmacokinetic advantages of glargine and detemir described elsewhere in the article are not clinical-outcome advantages.

text: How effective is one dose of measles vaccine at preventing measles, and how effective are two doses?
notes: One dose is about 93% effective, two doses about 97% effective. Traps: the same article separately gives 85% immunity after a dose at nine months and 95% after a dose at twelve months, which are seroconversion-by-age figures rather than the one/two-dose effectiveness pair. Citing polio's 90%/99% IPV antibody figures or BCG's 50% would be the wrong vaccine entirely.

text: Which countries remain polio-endemic with wild poliovirus, and at what age does the WHO recommend the first measles vaccine dose where measles is common?
notes: Requires joining two documents: Afghanistan and Pakistan are the only polio-endemic countries (as of August 2020), while the WHO recommends the first measles dose at nine months of age where measles is common and twelve months where it is not. Trap: measles was declared eliminated from the US in 2000 and polio eliminated in the Americas by 1994, so an engine may conflate elimination with eradication, or answer the schedule question from the polio document's 6-week OPV schedule.

text: Which Ariane rocket variant launched the James Webb Space Telescope, and when did the Ariane 6 make its first flight?
notes: Webb launched on an Ariane 5 (Ariane flight VA256) on 25 December 2021 - explicitly NOT an Ariane 6, which did not fly until 9 July 2024, more than two years later. Needs the JWST and Ariane 6 documents. This is the sharpest collision in the set: an engine that cites the Ariane 6 article for Webb's launch vehicle is citing a rocket that had not yet flown.

text: When did Falcon 9's first Commercial Resupply mission to the International Space Station launch, and how many SpaceX Dragon missions has the ISS received in total?
notes: Joins two documents: the first Commercial Resupply mission launched on October 8, 2012 (Falcon 9 article), and the ISS article's flight tally lists 52 SpaceX Dragon missions. Trap: Flight 3, Dragon C2+ was the first cargo delivery to the ISS but was a demonstration rather than the first operational Commercial Resupply mission (Flight 4, CRS-1); and the 95 Progress / 73 Soyuz counts belong to other vehicles.

text: What is the advertised price of a Falcon 9 Block 5 launch, and what are SpaceX's estimated internal costs per launch?
notes: Contested cost picture: the advertised Block 5 price is $74 million in 2026, while SpaceX's internal costs as of 2024 are estimated between $15 million and $28 million, with the expendable second stage alone costing $12 million to produce. Government prices differ again ($95 million for US Air Force launches, $133 million for Dragon cargo missions). ULA's Tory Bruno says ten flights are needed to break even on reusability while Musk claims breakeven after two. Trap: citing Ariane 6's projected launch prices exceeding EUR 100 million as the Falcon 9 price.

text: At what altitude does the International Space Station orbit, and how long has it been continuously inhabited?
notes: About 400 kilometres (250 miles) above Earth, and continuously inhabited for 25 years and 334 days since 2 November 2000. The duration is a snapshot and must be dated to be complete. Traps: the article also gives a minimum mean altitude of 370 km and a maximum of 460 km, and notes the nominal orbit was raised from about 350 km to about 400 km after Shuttle retirement; Hubble's 540 km orbit belongs to a different document.

text: How many individuals, from how many countries, have visited the International Space Station, and as of what date?
notes: The article gives two snapshots that disagree: 290 individuals from 26 countries as of August 2025, and a total of 294 individuals from 26 countries as of 14 February 2026. An undated single number cannot be fully supported; a complete answer dates the figure and ideally notes both snapshots. Trap: the 13 self-funded visitors and the US/Russia breakdown (172 and 65) are subsets, not the total.

text: How much has Europe invested in the development of Ariane 6 and its launch site, as of what date, and what per-launch subsidy did the ESA Director General cite?
notes: About EUR 3.6 billion as of August 2026; ESA Director General Josef Aschbacher said that at a rate of nine flights per year European governments would need to subsidise each launch by between EUR 32 and 38 million. The investment figure is explicitly dated, so an undated answer is incomplete. Trap: the 2015 estimate of EUR 2.815 billion of government funds plus EUR 400 million industry share is an earlier snapshot, and the separate EUR 340 million annual subsidy from the 16th to the 42nd flight is a different number.

text: Is BCG vaccination recommended during pregnancy, and what did the WHO decide in 2007 about giving BCG to infants with HIV?
notes: Both halves assert absence: BCG is not recommended for use during pregnancy because there is insufficient evidence about its safety there (although no harmful effects on the fetus have been observed), and in 2007 the WHO stopped recommending BCG for infants with HIV even where the risk of tuberculosis exposure is high, because of a disseminated BCG infection risk of roughly 400 per 100,000. Trap: the measles article says its vaccine is generally safe even for those infected by HIV, so citing that for BCG is the wrong vaccine. A reactive tuberculin skin test is also a contraindication, but a different one.
aspects: not recommended for use during pregnancy

text: Have rates of autism, Guillain-Barre syndrome or inflammatory bowel disease been found to increase after measles vaccination, and what became of the Wakefield paper?
notes: The correct answer asserts absence: rates of Guillain-Barre syndrome, autism and inflammatory bowel disease do not appear to be increased by measles vaccination. Wakefield's 1998 Lancet paper was retracted and fraudulent, and he was found 'dishonest' by the General Medical Council and barred from practising medicine in the UK. Trap: the article does document real adverse effects (fever, rash, anaphylaxis at about 3.5-10 cases per million doses), and citing those as support for the autism claim is unsupported.
aspects: do not appear to be increased

text: Which two countries have never used BCG routinely, and what approach do they rely on instead?
notes: The United States and the Netherlands have never used BCG routinely, relying instead on a reliable Mantoux test to accurately detect and treat disease, given the relative rarity of tuberculosis. The correct answer asserts the absence of a practice. Trap: Australia and New Zealand phased BCG out but did once use it, so they are not the answer; and the polio article's US mass immunisation campaigns concern a different vaccine.

text: How is one international unit of insulin defined by mass, and who set the first definition of an insulin unit and in what year?
notes: One international unit (1 IU) is the biological equivalent of 34.7 micrograms of pure crystalline insulin; the first definition, the amount required to induce hypoglycemia in a rabbit, was set by James Collip at the University of Toronto in 1922. Trap: the old USP unit, defined as the amount reducing a fasting rabbit's blood glucose to 45 mg/dL, is a later and different definition, and the 1973 U-100 standardisation concerns concentration, not the unit itself.

text: By how much did reported annual polio cases fall between 1988 and 2018, and what is the stated rate of vaccine-associated paralytic poliomyelitis from oral polio vaccine?
notes: Cases fell from an estimated 350,000 in 1988 to 33 in 2018. The VAPP rate is stated inconsistently within the same document: 'about three cases of vaccine-associated paralytic poliomyelitis per million doses given' in the summary versus 'roughly one individual per every 2.7 million doses administered' later, and that disagreement is part of the answer. Trap: the 5,000 cases per million who are paralysed following a polio infection is a comparison figure, not a vaccine rate.

text: On what date, and aboard which launch vehicle, was Voyager 1 launched?
notes: Launched on September 5, 1977 from Launch Complex 41 at Cape Canaveral Air Force Station aboard a Titan IIIE launch vehicle. Trap: Voyager 2 launched earlier, on August 20, 1977, and the article says Voyager 1 went up 16 days after its twin; an engine may also wrongly attach a modern launcher from the Falcon 9 or Ariane 6 documents, or credit the Centaur upper stage as the launch vehicle.
